questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has a 1 week history of a deep, boring pain in her right eye that keeps her awake at night. Moving her eye makes it much worse. The eye is diffusely violet-red and tender to touch through the lid. Visual acuity is 6/12 in the right eye. Her CRP is 38 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe pain worse on eye movement in a violet tender eye in a patient with RA is scleritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Moving her eye makes it much worse
steps.x: **RA** + severe deep pain **worse with eye movement** + **violet** tender globe + reduced vision = scleritis.

elim: Gives a fixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy cornea and headache with vomiting, not tenderness and pain on eye movement.
Gives photophobia and ciliary flush with a small pupil; pain is not typically worse on eye movement with a violet, tender globe.
Gritty discomfort with purulent discharge and normal vision; not deep severe pain.
Milder, not tender, pain not worse with movement, and it does not reduce vision.

steps.x: **E. Scleritis.** Scleritis: severe pain worse on eye movement, deep red/violet, tender, autoimmune background.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a 4 day history of a severely painful red left eye. The pain spreads to her left jaw and cheek and is worse when she looks around. She has photophobia. The sclera is deep red over a wide area and tender. The cornea is clear and the pupil reacts normally.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Eye pain radiating to the jaw and face, worse with movement, in a patient with SLE is scleritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: spreads to her left jaw and cheek
steps.x: Scleritis pain can **radiate to the jaw or face**, and SLE is a recognised association.

elim: Explains jaw pain but not a deep red, tender eye with photophobia.
Gives jaw claudication and sudden visual loss in older patients, not a red, tender sclera.
Gives a dermatomal vesicular rash on the forehead and nose tip.
Painless, flat bright-red patch with normal vision.

steps.x: **D. Scleritis.** Radiating jaw/face pain plus pain on eye movement points to scleritis.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man with ulcerative colitis has a mildly uncomfortable red right eye for 2 days. The eye waters a little but vision is normal. There is a wedge-shaped patch of bright red injection on the nasal bulbar conjunctiva. Moving the eye does not change the discomfort. He asks how this differs from the scleritis his aunt had.
questions.q: Which feature of scleritis would most help distinguish it from his condition?
o: Severe pain worse on eye movement
questions.e: Scleritis is more serious than episcleritis: severe pain that worsens with eye movement is the key differentiator. Segmental injection, watering and ulcerative colitis fit episcleritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which feature of scleritis would most help distinguish it from his condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
This is **episcleritis** (UC, segmental, watering, mild). The question asks what would mark **scleritis** instead.

elim: This is classically linked to episcleritis (ulcerative colitis), so it does not favour scleritis.
Vision is often reduced in scleritis; normal acuity fits episcleritis.
A segmental pattern of bulbar injection is typical of episcleritis.
Watering is a feature of episcleritis.

steps.x: **D. Severe pain worse on eye movement.** Key differentiator: scleritis pain is severe and worse with eye movement.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with granulomatosis with polyangiitis has a painful red left eye that is worse on eye movement. In eye casualty, topical phenylephrine 10% is instilled into the left eye. After 15 minutes the deep bluish-red vessels remain engorged and the redness is unchanged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Phenylephrine blanches superficial episcleral vessels but not the deep vascular plexus inflamed in scleritis, so persistent redness confirms scleritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**No blanching** with phenylephrine = deep scleral vessels involved.

elim: Itchy, bilateral, with chemosis; superficial vessels would blanch.
Painless blood under the conjunctiva, not engorged vessels.
Superficial episcleral vessels blanch with phenylephrine.
A painless fibrovascular wedge growing onto the cornea.

steps.x: **E. Scleritis.** Phenylephrine test: blanches in episcleritis, not in scleritis.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with 25 years of rheumatoid arthritis has had scleritis in her right eye for 4 months. On examination there is a large area of thin sclera through which the dark uvea shows as a bluish-grey patch. Her vision in that eye has fallen from 6/9 to 6/24.
questions.q: Which complication is she at most risk of?
questions.e: Bluish uvea showing through thinned sclera is scleromalacia, which can progress to globe rupture in severe necrotising scleritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which complication is she at most risk of? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Thin sclera showing uvea = **scleromalacia**, the step before perforation.

elim: Not a complication of scleral thinning.
A developmental corneal ectasia, unrelated to scleral inflammation.
Infection of the orbit with fever and proptosis, not a result of scleromalacia.
Inherited rod-cone dystrophy, not inflammatory.

steps.x: **B. Globe rupture.** Complications of scleritis: vision loss, scleral thinning and, rarely, globe rupture.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has a 3 day history of a severely painful, tender red left eye that is worse on eye movement. Over the past 2 months he has had recurrent nosebleeds, nasal crusting and a cough with blood-streaked sputum. Urinalysis shows blood 3+ and protein 2+.
questions.q: Which underlying condition is most likely to be causing his eye problem?
questions.e: ENT, lung and renal involvement suggest granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a vasculitis; scleritis is often its extra-ocular/extra-articular manifestation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which underlying condition is most likely to be causing his eye problem? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Upper airway + lung + kidney = small-vessel **vasculitis** (GPA). Scleritis is a recognised manifestation.

elim: Linked to anterior uveitis, with back pain rather than ENT, lung and renal disease.
Can cause orbital cellulitis, not an autoimmune scleritis with haematuria.
Causes uveitis and hilar nodes; ENT crusting with haematuria suggests a small-vessel vasculitis.
Associated with episcleritis, not this multisystem picture.

steps.x: **E. Vasculitis.** Scleritis associations: rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis and SLE.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a 5 day history of a severely painful right eye. She cannot tolerate bright light and her vision is blurred. The right eye is deep red and tender. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on blood tests?
o: Low complement C3 and C4 only
questions.e: Scleritis presents with pain, photophobia, reduced vision, a tender deep red eye and raised inflammatory markers, reflecting the underlying systemic autoimmune disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on blood tests? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Tender deep red eye with photophobia in RA = scleritis, which comes with **raised inflammatory markers**.

elim: Suggests active SLE nephritis, not the expected marker change here.
Not a feature of scleritis.
Scleritis typically raises inflammatory markers, unlike benign episcleritis.
Indicates pancreatitis.

steps.x: **D. Raised ESR and CRP.** Scleritis: raised ESR/CRP reflects systemic inflammation.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman has a red left eye for 3 days. She describes a severe ache that is much worse when she reads and moves her eyes from line to line. The redness is diffuse with a violaceous hue. She has a 2 year history of symmetrical small joint pain in her hands.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A violaceous, diffusely red eye with severe pain worse on eye movement and an inflammatory arthritis is scleritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: much worse when she reads and moves her eyes
steps.x: Severe pain **worse with eye movement** + **violaceous** colour + probable RA = scleritis.

elim: Gritty, itchy lid margins with crusting; no severe ache.
Mild discomfort not worsened by movement, usually segmental bright redness.
Gives foreign body sensation, discharge and a corneal opacity, often in contact lens wearers.
Pain on eye movement but a white eye with visual loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect.

steps.x: **E. Scleritis.** Pain worse on eye movement with a RED eye: scleritis. With a WHITE eye: think optic neuritis.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with rheumatoid arthritis has a red right eye. He is worried because his daughter, who has ulcerative colitis, had a red eye last year that settled on its own within 2 weeks without treatment. His own eye is diffusely deep red, very tender and painful on eye movement, and his vision has dropped.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate description of his condition compared with his daughter's?
o: Infective and treated with topical antibiotics
Managed by routine GP review in 6 weeks
More serious, needing same-day specialist care
questions.e: His picture is scleritis, which is more serious than episcleritis (UC-associated and self-resolving) and needs same-day ophthalmology.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate description of his condition compared with his daughter's? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Daughter: **episcleritis** (UC, self-limiting). Him: **scleritis** (RA, pain on movement, visual loss).

elim: Episcleritis (his daughter's) usually resolves alone; scleritis does not.
Scleritis is immune-mediated, not infective.
Lubricants suit episcleritis, not sight-threatening scleritis.
Scleritis is an ophthalmological emergency.

steps.x: **E. More serious, needing same-day specialist care.** Scleritis is more serious than episcleritis and is an ophthalmological emergency.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been treated for scleritis for 6 months. Her right eye remains painful and red. She now has difficulty reading and recognising faces with that eye. Visual acuity is 6/36 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her worsening vision?
questions.e: Vision loss is a recognised complication of scleritis, alongside scleral thinning and, rarely, globe rupture.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her worsening vision? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: has been treated for scleritis for 6 months
steps.x: Ongoing painful red eye + falling acuity = sight loss from the scleritis itself.

elim: Would not explain a persistently painful red eye.
A childhood developmental problem, not acquired at 72.
Objective acuity loss in a painful red eye is organic.
Would not be accompanied by pain and redness; corrects with a pinhole.

steps.x: **C. Complication of scleritis.** Scleritis threatens vision; it is not a cosmetic red eye.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with no past medical history is diagnosed with scleritis in eye casualty. She mentions morning stiffness in her hands, a facial rash in sunlight and mouth ulcers. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood investigation?
questions.e: Scleritis is strongly associated with RA, SLE and vasculitis, so bloods are ESR/CRP and an autoimmune screen (RF, anti-CCP, ANA, ANCA).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate blood investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Possible SLE/RA behind new scleritis: look for the **systemic autoimmune cause**.

elim: Scleritis is not infective in this picture.
Diabetes is not linked to scleritis.
Sarcoid is a uveitis association; a single test misses RA, SLE and vasculitis.
Thyroid eye disease gives lid retraction and proptosis, not this.

steps.x: **B. ESR, CRP and autoimmune screen.** Scleritis bloods: ESR/CRP plus autoimmune screen.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with rheumatoid arthritis sees his GP with a 2 day history of a very painful red left eye that is worse on eye movement and tender. Vision is reduced to 6/18. The GP has no slit lamp. His temperature is 37.0°C and pulse rate 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Trial of topical chloramphenicol and review in 1 week
questions.e: Suspected scleritis is an ophthalmological emergency, so the first-line step is same-day ophthalmology assessment with slit-lamp examination.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: worse on eye movement and tender
The GP has no slit lamp
steps.x: Painful tender red eye worse on movement with reduced vision = suspected scleritis = **same day** eye review.

elim: Not the first step; the diagnosis is clinical by an ophthalmologist.
This is not infective conjunctivitis.
Scleritis is an emergency; routine referral delays sight-saving treatment.
Delays treatment of an ophthalmological emergency.

steps.x: **D. Same-day ophthalmology assessment.** First-line in scleritis: same-day ophthalmology assessment.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a red, uncomfortable right eye. The ophthalmologist cannot decide clinically between scleritis and episcleritis. Her visual acuity is 6/6. Her temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which bedside test would best distinguish the two?
questions.e: Phenylephrine blanches the superficial episcleral vessels in episcleritis but not the deep scleral plexus inflamed in scleritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which bedside test would best distinguish the two? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: cannot decide clinically between scleritis and episcleritis
steps.x: The classic bedside discriminator is the **phenylephrine blanching** test.

elim: Shows corneal epithelial defects, not depth of vascular involvement.
Measures tear production for dry eye.
Measures intraocular pressure, which does not separate the two.
A mydriatic with no effect on vessel blanching.

steps.x: **D. Topical phenylephrine drops.** Blanches = episcleritis; persists = scleritis.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has a second episode of scleritis. He has no joint or skin symptoms. Investigations show: ESR 64 mm/h (<20), CRP 41 mg/L (<5), creatinine 168 µmol/L (60–110). Urinalysis: blood 2+, protein 2+.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Scleritis with active urinary sediment and rising creatinine suggests ANCA vasculitis, so ANCA is the key part of the autoimmune screen.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Scleritis + nephritic urine = think **vasculitis** behind it.

elim: Used in type 1 diabetes.
Tests for spondyloarthropathy in uveitis, not this renal-eye picture.
Iron studies do not explain scleritis with nephritis.
Thyroid autoimmunity does not cause scleritis with nephritis.

steps.x: **A. ANCA.** In scleritis always screen for the systemic cause: RA, SLE, vasculitis.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis phones NHS 111 with a 1 day history of a severely painful red right eye. The pain wakes her and is worse when she moves the eye. She says her vision is blurred. She has no history of trauma.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Book a GP appointment within 2 weeks
Buy chloramphenicol drops from a pharmacy
questions.e: Suspected scleritis is an ophthalmological emergency, so first line is same-day or urgent referral to ophthalmology.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: worse when she moves the eye
steps.x: Severe pain worse on movement + RA + blurred vision = suspected scleritis.

elim: Too slow for an ophthalmological emergency.
Not infective conjunctivitis.
Scleritis needs same-day ophthalmology.
Does not treat a sight-threatening condition.

steps.x: **D. Same-day referral to eye casualty.** First line: urgent/same-day ophthalmology referral (NICE CKS Red eye).

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has non-necrotising diffuse anterior scleritis confirmed in eye casualty. His pain is moderate, there is no scleral thinning and his vision is 6/6. He has no history of peptic ulcer or renal disease. His temperature is 36.9°C and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Milder scleritis is treated with systemic NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or flurbiprofen; steroids are for severe disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Mild, non-necrotising disease = **systemic NSAID**.

elim: Reserved for severe or necrotising disease.
Antiviral; scleritis is not herpetic here.
Antibiotic drops do not treat immune-mediated scleritis.
Do not control scleral inflammation.

steps.x: **C. Oral ibuprofen.** Mild scleritis: oral NSAID (ibuprofen or flurbiprofen 100 mg TDS).

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has necrotising scleritis of her left eye. There is an avascular white patch of sclera with surrounding inflammation, and her vision has fallen to 6/36. She took oral flurbiprofen for a week without improvement.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Severe or necrotising scleritis needs systemic corticosteroids, oral prednisolone or pulsed IV methylprednisolone, to prevent perforation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Necrotising + falling vision + NSAID failure = **severe** disease.

elim: NSAIDs have failed and are inadequate for necrotising disease.
Not an infection.
Topical steroid alone does not control scleritis.
A diagnostic test, not a treatment.

steps.x: **C. Pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone.** Severe scleritis: high-dose systemic steroid, often pulsed IV methylprednisolone.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has had three episodes of scleritis in 18 months. Each responds to oral prednisolone but flares when the dose falls below 15 mg daily. Her joints are also active. Her BMI is 29 kg/m² and she has new impaired fasting glucose.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Scleritis with an active underlying autoimmune disease is controlled with immunosuppressants under specialist care, sparing steroid side effects.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: flares when the dose falls below 15 mg
steps.x: Steroid-dependent, recurrent, active RA = treat the **underlying disease** with a steroid-sparing agent.

elim: Do not control scleritis or her RA, and raise IOP.
Steroid side effects are already appearing; a steroid-sparing agent is needed.
Inadequate for recurrent steroid-dependent disease.
A diagnostic test only.

steps.x: **D. Specialist-led immunosuppressant therapy.** Underlying autoimmune disease: immunosuppressants under specialist care.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with SLE has diffuse scleritis. He was started on oral flurbiprofen 100 mg three times a day 2 weeks ago. His pain is now worse and his vision has fallen from 6/6 to 6/18. There is no scleral thinning. His eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Failure of systemic NSAIDs with falling vision marks severe disease, needing systemic corticosteroid such as oral prednisolone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: flurbiprofen 100 mg three times a day
steps.x: NSAID failure + visual drop = escalate to **systemic steroid**.

elim: Gastroprotection does not address treatment failure.
Not infective.
Changing NSAID does not escalate treatment of worsening disease.
Antibiotic drops have no role.

steps.x: **C. Oral prednisolone.** Ladder: NSAID (mild) to systemic steroid (severe) to immunosuppressant (underlying disease).

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a scleral biopsy taken during surgery for necrotising scleritis. Histology shows a dense inflammatory infiltrate within the sclera with epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her scleral inflammation?
questions.e: Scleritis is a granulomatous, T-cell mediated inflammatory infiltrate within the sclera, often an extra-articular feature of autoimmune disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her scleral inflammation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells
steps.x: Epithelioid and giant cells = **granuloma** = T-cell (type IV) driven inflammation.

elim: No organisms; granulomas with an autoimmune history point to immune inflammation.
Type I allergy gives itchy conjunctivitis.
There is a dense inflammatory infiltrate.
Would show viral inclusions, not granulomas.

steps.x: **B. Granulomatous T-cell mediated inflammation.** Scleritis pathology: granulomatous, T-cell mediated infiltrate.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with scleritis asks why her eye hurts so much more than the episcleritis she had years ago. She describes a deep, boring pain that wakes her at night. Her ophthalmologist explains the anatomy.
questions.q: Which best explains why the pain in scleritis is so severe?
o: Inflamed rigid sclera stretches the nerve-rich episclera
Sclera is highly vascular and bleeds
questions.e: The sclera is relatively avascular and rigid, so swelling stretches the nerve-rich episclera and presses on surrounding structures, causing intense pain.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best explains why the pain in scleritis is so severe? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Rigid, avascular tissue cannot expand, so swelling stretches the surrounding nerves.

elim: That is keratitis or abrasion pain.
That is acute angle-closure glaucoma.
The sclera is relatively avascular.
Superficial vessel dilation is mild, as in conjunctivitis.

steps.x: **B. Inflamed rigid sclera stretches the nerve-rich episclera.** Severe pain: rigid avascular sclera + stretched nerve-rich episclera.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and rheumatoid nodules develops necrotising scleritis with scleral thinning. His ophthalmologist warns him the eye could perforate.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the scleral necrosis?
o: Immune complex vasculitis causing scleral ischaemia
questions.e: In RA, chronic immune complex deposition and vasculitis cause ischaemia and necrosis of the sclera; the thinned sclera (scleromalacia) can rupture.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of the scleral necrosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
RA + necrosis = **immune complex vasculitis** starving the sclera of blood.

elim: Necrotising scleritis in RA is immune-mediated.
Raised IOP does not cause scleral necrosis.
Allergy does not cause necrosis.
Methotrexate treats, not causes, scleritis.

steps.x: **D. Immune complex vasculitis causing scleral ischaemia.** Necrotising scleritis: immune complex vasculitis, ischaemia, scleromalacia, rupture.

questions.stem: A medical student watches an ophthalmologist instil phenylephrine into two patients with red eyes. In the first, the redness fades within 15 minutes. In the second, who has granulomatosis with polyangiitis and pain on eye movement, the redness persists.
questions.q: Which best explains the persistent redness in the second patient?
o: Inflammation of the deep scleral vascular plexus
questions.e: Scleritis involves the deeper vascular plexus, which topical phenylephrine does not reach or constrict, unlike the superficial vessels of episcleritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best explains the persistent redness in the second patient? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Phenylephrine constricts **superficial** vessels only. Persistent redness = deep vessels.

elim: Subconjunctival haemorrhage does not cause pain on eye movement.
This is what blanches, as in the first patient.
Not the mechanism.
Not relevant to blanching.

steps.x: **C. Inflammation of the deep scleral vascular plexus.** Scleritis = deep plexus; episcleritis = superficial vessels.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has scleritis. Her ophthalmologist asks the rheumatology team to review her, explaining that the eye is often a window to a systemic disease. She has hand joint swelling and positive anti-CCP antibodies.
questions.q: Which best describes her scleritis?
o: Primary eye disease unrelated to her joints
questions.e: Scleritis is often an extra-articular manifestation of a systemic autoimmune or vasculitic disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best describes her scleritis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Anti-CCP + joint swelling = RA; the scleritis is part of it.

elim: Anti-CCP is a diagnostic marker, not a drug.
Scleritis here is immune-mediated.
Scleritis is heavily associated with systemic autoimmune disease.
UC is associated with episcleritis.

steps.x: **B. Extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis.** Scleritis is an extra-articular manifestation of RA, vasculitis or SLE.
